label: Marketing brochure
description: Lead marketing image. The envelope, footprint and camera are fixed; the facade architecture is designed by the provider rather than copied from the massing study.
intent: Produce the lead marketing photograph for this industrial project: the single image that goes on the cover of the brochure and sells the development. It must read as a real photograph of a genuinely well-designed building, shot by an architectural photographer on the best day of the year.
allowed_changes: Design the envelope, then photograph it. Compose the cladding into fields with real proportion rather than uniform sheeting: vary panel module, orientation and tone where the building changes use, and let the structural bay rhythm show as depth. Give the office and entrance volume genuine architectural presence — glazing that reads as workplace daylight, a defined canopy or portal, a legible address. Set brise-soleil, louvres, deep reveals and a durable plinth where a building in this climate would want them. Bring the whole scene to full photographic quality: material identity and micro-texture, panel joints, fasteners, flashings, sealant lines, honest weathering, real light transport with directional sun, bounce, occlusion in recesses, contact shadows, and glazing that reflects sky with correct fresnel. Resolve landscape into real species with real growth habit inside its authored zones. Populate the site for a working day with correctly scaled vehicles, equipment and people that never hide architecture or block access.
photography: Full-frame architectural photography with a perspective-corrected tilt-shift lens, verticals true. Choose the best light this fixed camera can be given: clear high-pressure day, strong directional sun raking across the facade so the bay rhythm and panel relief read as shadow, deep blue sky with sculptural cloud, and shadows that stay open and coloured rather than crushing to black. Highlight roll-off must hold detail in bright metal roofing. Sharp across the subject with natural lens falloff and real atmospheric perspective into the distance. Profiled metal shows fine seams, real fixings and shallow surface waviness, never smooth plastic planes. Concrete and asphalt show aggregate, saw joints, drainage falls and restrained tyre wear. The finished frame should be indistinguishable from a published photograph in an industrial development brochure.
context_direction: The estate around the project is real and recently built: sealed roads with kerbs and line marking, neighbouring lots with their own hardstanding and sheds, boundary fences, verges, service infrastructure and mature planting, continuing to a hazy industrial horizon. Resolve every flat or translucent placeholder volume into a believable neighbouring building; never let a grey slab survive into the final image. Keep the surroundings clearly secondary to the project.
prohibited: No fantasy colour, no surreal lighting, no impossible structure, no showroom emptiness where a working site would have activity. Signage must be generic and invented, never a real company name or logo.
